title: Minimal Sorting Networks
origin: Sorting networks are fixed sequences of compare-and-swap operations that sort any input regardless of the data. Finding the smallest network (fewest comparators) for n inputs is a long-standing open problem going back to the 1960s. Knuth devoted an entire section of The Art of Computer Programming to it. For n up to 12, optimal sizes have been proven by SAT solvers and formal verification. For n = 13 through 20 and beyond, gaps remain between the best known constructions and the proven lower bounds. Improving any of these records, even by a single comparator, would be a publishable result.
instance: A sorting network on n wires is an ordered list of comparator pairs (i, j) with 1 <= i < j <= n. Each comparator examines wires i and j and swaps their values if out of order. A network is valid if it correctly sorts every possible input. By the 0-1 principle (Knuth, 1973), it suffices to check all 2^n binary input strings. For any n >= 13 where the best known size exceeds the proven lower bound, find a valid sorting network that uses fewer comparators than the current record. Depth is tracked as a secondary metric. See the leaderboard below for specific gaps at each n.

scoring.summary: Primary metric is comparator count (size). Lower is better. Depth is a secondary metric for tie-breaking and Pareto tracking.

metrics.name: Comparator count (size)
metrics.description: Total number of comparator pairs in the network. Lower is better. Beating the current best known size at any n is the goal.

metrics.name: Depth
metrics.description: Number of parallel layers when non-conflicting comparators are grouped. Lower depth means faster parallel execution. At some n values, optimal depth is known even when optimal size is not.

metrics.name: Correctness fraction
metrics.description: Fraction of the 2^n binary inputs the network sorts correctly. Must be 100% for a valid submission. Partial scores track progress.

scoring.note: Any valid network that beats the current best known size at any n >= 13 would be a new record.

warmup.title: Warm-up: 4-input sorting network
warmup.body: Sort 4 inputs using 5 comparators. One optimal solution: [(1,2), (3,4), (1,3), (2,4), (2,3)]. First layer: compare wires 1-2 and 3-4 in parallel. Second layer: compare 1-3 and 2-4. Third layer: compare 2-3. This is provably optimal (S(4) = 5). Verify it sorts all 2^4 = 16 binary inputs.

verification: For each submission: (1) Check that all comparator pairs (i,j) satisfy 1 <= i < j <= n, (2) Simulate the network on all 2^n binary input strings using the 0-1 principle, (3) For each input, apply comparators in order (swap if out of order) and check the output is non-decreasing. If all inputs produce sorted output, the network is valid. (4) Count comparators for size, compute greedy layering for depth. Full verification runs in seconds for n up to 20.

bounds.label: 0-1 principle
bounds.name: Binary test is sufficient
bounds.formula: A network sorts all inputs over any totally ordered set if and only if it sorts all 2^n binary strings (Knuth, TAOCP Vol. 3, 1973).

bounds.label: Open gaps
bounds.name: n = 13 through 20+
bounds.formula: For each of these sizes, the best known construction exceeds the proven lower bound. The leaderboard shows the current gap at each n. Closing any gap by even one comparator is a new result.

bounds.label: Depth bounds
bounds.name: Optimal depth known for some n
bounds.formula: Ehlers and Muller proved optimal depths for several values of n (e.g., D(17)=10). At those sizes, depth is settled and size is the remaining open question.

leaderboard.note: Best known size-depth trade-offs from Dobbelaere's maintained table (accessed 2026-04-20; table update 2025-11-07), with foundational proofs from Codish et al., Bundala et al., Ehlers & Muller, and Harder.

suggestedApproach.title: Verify the 4-input warm-up
suggestedApproach.body: Write code to simulate the 5-comparator network on all 16 binary inputs. Confirm it sorts every one. This gives you the core verification loop for any n.

suggestedApproach.title: Pick a target n
suggestedApproach.body: Check the leaderboard for where the gap between the best known size and lower bound is largest. Larger gaps mean more room for improvement. n = 13-16 are more computationally tractable; n = 17-20 have bigger gaps but harder search spaces.

suggestedApproach.title: SAT encoding
suggestedApproach.body: Encode the problem as a Boolean satisfiability instance with variables for which comparators to include and clauses enforcing all binary inputs are sorted. Symmetry-breaking constraints reduce the search space substantially.

suggestedApproach.title: Start from known good networks
suggestedApproach.body: Download the current best network for your target n from Dobbelaere's tables. Try removing one comparator at a time and checking if the result still sorts all inputs. This rarely works directly but builds intuition for which comparators are essential.

suggestedApproach.title: Evolutionary search with local optimization
suggestedApproach.body: Generate random networks slightly larger than needed, verify them, then try to remove redundant comparators. Valsalam and Miikkulainen used crossover and mutation over network structures to find good results.

suggestedApproach.title: Prefix optimization
suggestedApproach.body: Fix the first few layers (which tend to be well-understood) and search only over the remaining layers. Ehlers and Muller used this to find depth-optimal networks.

agentPrompt: Find a sorting network that beats a current record. A sorting network is an ordered list of comparator pairs (i,j) where each comparator swaps wires i and j if out of order. By the 0-1 principle, you only need to verify all 2^n binary strings. Pick any n from 13 to 20 where the best known size has not been proven optimal (see the leaderboard for current gaps). Start from the best known network for your chosen n (available at Dobbelaere's table) and try to remove or rearrange comparators. A SAT-based approach also works well: encode the constraints and search for solutions with fewer comparators. Report the result as JSON with fields n and comparators (array of [i,j] pairs, 1-indexed).
